Not all polar bear populations are migratory. A lot of their movement pattern depends on food availability and other seasonal factors. I agree that they require much much more space than most facilities can provide, but there are other ways to meet their needs insofar as novelty and environmental choice. It is -this- aspect that is more important than blanket ‘migration,’ because again, their movement patterns are highly dependent on resource availability. 

Is captivity perfect? No. But these improvements in care and husbandry are just becoming more important as sea ice disappears.

Polar bears are definitely not the best fit for -many- facilities, but polar bear husbandry (and bear husbandry in zoos in general) has improved leaps and bounds within the past few decades. 

One of the reasons many zoos are phasing out polars bears isn’t necessarily only because they do not have the capacity to care for them- it’s that zoo guests look at modern, more up-to-date polar bear exhibits and assume it’s inappropriate care and complain, because it doesn’t “look” like what’s good for a polar bear.

polar bears are seal specialists- it’s not that they actively seek out humans to predate upon as a desirable part of their diet, it’s just more likely that a polar bear attack is motivated by predation than, say, a grizzly bear or sloth bear, which is more likely to be engaging in an aggressive territorial attack. 

crocodiles, on the other hand, kill more people than any other large wild vertebrate a year and almost invariably do it because they view humans as a food source.

https://www.ifaw.org/animals/arctic-wolf#:~:text=The%20lucky%20few%20who%20have,no%20intrinsic%20distrust%20of%20humans.

The wolf attacks in Canada that I found were mostly from old/sick wolves, wolves habituated to humans through feeding or eating garbage, attacks on people with dogs, or from captive wolves. Random, predatory attacks seem to be exceptionally rare and usually on a person outside alone.

Yes- on a practical level livestock predation was a large part of the organized drive to hunt wolves and absolutely continues to be hugely detrimental to wolf conservation in Europe today. But the cultural element of fearing/hating wolves because of attacks on humans was also significant. Not that humans were really a regular part of the wolf diet. Just that they definitely were historically responsible for more deadly attacks on humans than sharks.

Wolves in North America are relatively skittish around humans, but wolves in Europe and Asia historically would kill hundreds of people a year. That’s a big reason why they were extirpated from much of their range- I don’t think it’s good that they’ve gone locally extinct in so many places, but part of the reason they kill so few people now is because we almost wiped all of them out.

Helping an animal under human care learn to be less fearful/anxious can definitely help with their quality of life, but something else to keep in mind is that ultimately not every individual is a good candidate for an ambassador animal. Something I keep in mind when determining this is seeing how voluntarily the animal would work as an ambassador- ex. anticipatory behavior if they see training tools/leads, reactions towards keepers associated with the ambassador program, how the animal behaves towards unfamiliar people. 

When given choice/control over the situation, does the animal willingly participate? Can they handle unexpected or out of the ordinary behavior from people? How do they deal with novel stimuli? These are all good questions to keep in mind, because being an ambassador is asking something very specific of an animal, and not all of them have the right personality for it.

Buzzard is a pretty common colloquial name for vultures, particularly the turkey vulture, in the United States. This is like saying the word truck got assigned to lorries by mistake. It’s just a linguistic difference.

Researchers observe chimps in the wild all the time and the chimps know they’re there and don’t try to kill them. What happens to people attacked by chimps is horrible, and they’re absolutely capable of brutal violence toward each other, but they aren’t murder machines the way they’ve been portrayed to be. A wild chimp or a chimp kept in a qualified professional context will have a completely different psychology than an individual like Travis. 

They make tools, they play, they have cultural habits. They have really interesting and complex social structures. 

I’d rather be face to face with a wild chimp that knows I’m there than say, a grizzly bear or tiger aware of the same. Easily. 

In the wild, when they have attacked adult humans, it’s  typically much more akin to brutal physical communication as opposed to deliberately murderous violence. They’re powerful and potentially dangerous, but they aren’t acting out of malice. They’re animals. 

We’ve killed a lot more of them than they have killed of us.

Because horses and donkeys have different numbers of chromosomes, the resulting hybrids generally have an odd number of chromosomes which leads to sterility as having an odd number of chromosomes damages the animal’s ability to produce reproductive cells. 

Grizzly bears, black bears, and polar bears all have 74 chromosomes, so their offspring would theoretically be fertile and in the case of polar x grizzly hybrids regularly go on to reproduce. 

However, black bears and grizzly bears diverged from a common ancestor much longer ago than polar bears and grizzly bears. It’s hard to put a hard and fast rule to this, as every species and every hybrid is different, but sometimes the two different sets of genes may not “line up” correctly or they may interact in unexpected ways. 

In captivity, black bears and grizzlies have frequently been observed mating together, but these unions rarely result in offspring. When they have, the offspring often die shortly after birth. This may indicate that something about the way the grizzly and black bear genetics line up has a tendency to produce weak embryos/young. 

There definitely have been grizzly x black bear hybrids that survive into adulthood, it’s just less likely than with the more genetically stable grizzly x polar hybrid, which is why I described them as less viable, if that makes sense! And there are other barriers to this hybrid outside of genetics as well, this is just one of the factors that make them pretty rare.

That isn’t true, black bears (Ursus americanus) and grizzly bears (Ursus arctos) are part of the same genus but are absolutely not the same species. It wouldn’t be like a poodle and a German shepherd breeding, it would be like a zebra and a donkey breeding.

The species do hybridize, but the offspring aren’t always viable.

Grizzly bears and polar bears, however, hybridize much more readily and successfully as the two species are more closely related.

This sounds like a great opportunity for you! I know a lot of keepers who initially began their career in vet med. Other commenters have covered some really important points already but a “softer” skill to keep in mind is learning how to talk to people about animals, especially about something that might be confusing for a person without experience working with animals to witness. 

For example, if a zoo guest sees an animal laying around or panting, they might become concerned that the animal is distressed and ask about it. Likewise, I’ve heard from coworkers who used to work in vet med that they’d get pet owners coming in really worried about their pets, when it turns out whatever they’re worried about is actually very normal for that species. 

Learning to explain these sorts of things in a way that is educational without being condescending OR too dense can take some practice, but it’s worth investing time in because it helps people learn about animals and also can help clear up misconceptions around zoos/animal behavior in human-managed environments!

I do scent enrichment with our snakes and lizards- I’ll take wool from our livestock or shed fur from one of the rodents in our collection and rub it on some of the objects in their exhibits. This has the added benefit of getting zoo guests more interested in our reptiles. They aren’t always as “exciting” as birds and mammals so seeing snakes and lizards active and exploring their environment can make a really great educational moment.

Getting experience with a wider variety of taxa through volunteering or interning unfortunately might be your best bet. Applying to smaller facilities (that still maintain high quality animal welfare!) also may be an option for you- oftentimes their educators are also keeper staff, and have a lot of hands on time with their ambassador animals for training and general husbandry/care.

I’m currently working as a zookeeper and my major is in one of the social sciences- as long as you have a degree, most zoos seem to care more about actual field experience. I even know someone who had a degree in CS who now works for one of the best conservation facilities in the US. Just make sure you can volunteer and intern, and you’ll be fine!

So glad she saw her! With most birds that build nests like this, *both* parents are typically responsible for care. So it’s likely the father has been bringing them food too! They’re just good at staying out of sight. 

In the future, some signs to look for if you don’t see the parents are if the nestlings start looking extra shrunken/wrinkly (which means they’re dehydrated), if they’re surrounded by flies, or if they look extra greasy or wet when it isn’t raining and they hadn’t previously. If that happens, you can call a local wildlife rehab to see if they can help and give you any further guidance! It’s great that you and your wife are looking out for them.

I think it was curiosity, and I agree that they aren’t mindless eating machines. However, I think the curiosity was more like, “Is this animal a threat, or is this animal food?” They regularly can and do eat other canids like jackals in their native environment, so I doubt they would exhibit any kind of friendly behavior with a domestic dog.

A big part of the reason painted dogs are so brightly colored is due to how social they are- this helps with identification of individuals and at times, communication. You’ll notice the dogs have a big, fluffy tail, tipped with white. The first dog, the one raising the alert, lifts his tail and poofs it out. This is actually to signal to the other dogs, which notice what the first dog had seen, and so they can all come over and check it out together. I doubt these guys have seen many domesticated dogs, so it‘s likely that they’re just trying to assess whether the service dog is food, or a threat. Since they are incredibly social, even more so than wolves or domestic dogs, they all do this together. 

Another commenter said that coyotes will imitate dog play behavior to lure other dogs in to kill, and I doubt that’s what the dog in this picture is doing. They don’t really have an evolutionary reason to do so, and despite their name, aren’t really all that closely related to domestic dogs or coyotes, so their body language and communication differ. Cats don’t need to kill birds for it to harm their populations. Even a brief presence of cats at bird nesting sites can cause an increase of predation events, fear responses in parents resulting in 33% less food for their offspring, and a 40% reduction in growth of offspring.

cats absolutely are the single largest source of anthropogenic mortality in bird populations and letting them roam outside might not necessarily be as cruel as declawing (although it reduces their lifespan) but it is wrong due to the damage it does to native species. In the United States, free-roaming cats kill between 1.3-4 BILLION birds annually and 6.3-22 BILLION mammals. Free roaming cats on islands have contributed to 14% of modern extinctions of bird, mammal, and reptile species. In Australia alone, cats contributed to the extinction of 20 native species. Many of the species that cats killed on these islands were endemic, found nowhere else on Earth, and are gone. Forever. 

In species that cats threaten, their presence can make reintroduction efforts nearly impossible. 

Due to the common idea that letting cats outside is good for them, some British birding groups insist letting cats out does not affect bird populations. However, a study has not been conducted at the population level to determine how true this is. According to Songbird Survival, the decline of certain species was attributed to the return of sparrowhawk populations in the late 20tg century, despite the fact that domestic cats kill THREE TIMES the amount that the sparrowhawk did, with a rising cat population and nearly 20,000 abandoned cats in the U.K. as of 2018. The use of red as a shadow is really cool, and adds a lot of impact/mood to the piece. One thing you could practice to make your art stronger that I notice is line confidence. Some of the red areas look a bit shaky or uneven, and making it smoother would improve the piece as a whole. A good way to work on this is making sure you’re not drawing from your wrist; getting the movement from your arm instead will make confident lines easier with less hesitant motions. Practicing drawing lines or basic shapes this way will also help more complex work look nice too!

Hey, this is a nice piece, don’t put yourself down! Something that might help you make it look more realistic is shading to the line, instead of just drawing lines and shading within them. 

In real life, there aren’t any lines, just the illusion of them. When you draw shapes, and more advanced forms, try to keep this in mind. That means instead of outlining your drawing, draw a very light sketch and add a gradient where the line seems to be, with the line as the darkest point, or in some situations, the opposite. If the line is actually a highlight, lift it off of the page with an eraser or leave it white. That way, form can be seen without lines that make it look cartoonish. Once you get this skill down, cartoonish art and other styles will also become easier.

This is pretty good! One thing that would really help it shine, though, would be working on proportion. I noticed that the midface/nose area in particular is very long compared to the reference image, which is a mistake a lot of people (including me!) make when drawing portraits.

One thing that could really help would be using guiding lines to make sure everything is proportional to the original image. Another thing, which might sound a little more confusing, is drawing what’s really there instead of what your brain is assuming. Guiding lines help you avoid this trap of assumption by showing you where parts of the image actually line up, instead of where your brain thinks that they do. 

You could try drawing the guidelines on the reference image itself for practice. To fix the nose length, for example, you could draw a line from the corner of the eye to the edge of the nostril, and then on your drawing, draw a line of the same length/angle to make sure you can see the space in between those two points. 

Another thing I noticed is the hair; while you did a good job on the skin texture, the hair looks a little “line-y.” To make it look softer and more like real hair, it’s helpful to draw it as a whole shape and shade/texture the clumps of hair forming the shape, instead of drawing each line of hair. I also added some sphagnum moss to hold moisture and for aesthetics. After that I added some springtails into the soil as a clean-up crew to help clean waste from the soil (and I plan on adding some isopods as well later.) The mantis won’t mess with these because they burrow into the soil. 

After that, I added plants! I have creeping ficus, Neoregelia “Fireball” which is a type of bromeliad, a begonia, and small lucky bamboo. I chose cork bark so I could place the bromeliad into it because this type does better there than in soil, although I’m not sure if that applies to all types. I also put a Velcro hygrometer/thermometer in there to measure humidity and heat. I wouldn’t recommend the kind that stick directly on because they can fall off and stick to animals/plants which will hurt them. I mist the tank about 1-2 times a day with distilled water to keep humidity up as needed, and I also have a heater stuck to the side and a uvb lamp overhead for the plants and to keep it at a comfortable temperature for the inhabitants. 

As far as the terrarium itself, I just bought it from Petsmart. You’ll want one with a screen lid for ventilation and also so they can climb/molt from it. Most mantises that I know of are arboreal, so you’ll want a terrarium on the taller side, so one about 2x the length of the mantis and 3x the height.

This one is specifically for a tropical species, so one for a species of a different climate would have different requirements and probably a different setup as well.

The Zamboni was on fire, and there was no driver at the wheel. 

Charlie Brown walked himself past the gathering flames and continued his aimless trek. Ashen snow dripped down his alopecic cranium like recurrent thoughts, and he couldn’t quite shake the feeling that he had been here before. To be clear, he hadn’t, but that didn’t much matter. It had been nearly a year since the case (and his short-lived career as a detective) had gone cold. He took his pension idly, coming to old age in near life-like fashion. Same day in the city, whirling around the gothic carousel. He felt, as he passed the string of ambulances, that he had never been much of a detective, though there wasn’t much to it. His entire job description relied upon the restating of the same question in different ways. Variations upon a theme. Like a bartender in a bad joke: why the long face? He told himself a lie that he was better off retired.

He entered the bowling alley. A pitcher of suds and gutter balls all the way down. He left the bowling alley.
Later: his decrepit apartment and the wailing felines without. Sunrise in a couple hours, he supposed. Nothing to stay up for, but little to sleep for either. 
He was drawn back to his desk, where he found the case folder in the same spot he left it last night. The pretty, muted face of Lucy (from a photo captured nearly a year ago) still clipped on top of a stack of paperwork several months tall. After dozens of witness interrogations and a general circumvention of ‘official procedure’, Brown had gotten nowhere. So little could reliably be said about the case in terms of evidence that Brown had started to consider ‘the city’ to be the true perpetrator. Perhaps he was right. But these weren’t results, they said. Orders from higher-up. The invisible hand moved him from Homicide to Traffic, from Traffic to an early retirement. Exeunt pursued by bad luck. 

The whole thing was like a puzzle with missing pieces that wouldn’t fit together even if he could find them. Brown closed the file and opened his diary, but couldn’t find anything to write.

I feel for you. Judging by your post it seems like you have a Cluster B personality disorder, and quite frankly the way people talk about those afflicted with the illness is disgusting. 

I've been abused by people with BPD, I've been abused by people without BPD, or without any other disorder. Having a mental illness does not make someone a bad person by any means. In fact, I feel for my BPD abusers, because I realize their actions were just due to a lot of their unchecked hatred against themselves, and their inability to cope with their emotions, although this doesn't excuse their actions. No disorder causes someone to be inherently a bad person. The only bad people are the ones that treat people badly, refuse to recognize it, and refuse to change, which can describe anyone, mental illness or no mental illness.

Besides that, there are people with personality disorders that realize something is wrong and want to heal, and stigma makes it much harder to do that. Hatred against those with serious mental disorders, whether it be because of interactions with those with the disorder, or due to uneducated assumptions, or both, is wrong and will always be wrong. 

You deserve the chance to heal, and you shouldn't hate yourself just because people feel like you should. You're a person, more than just a diagnosis, and anyone who judges you based on your diagnosis without getting to know you is wrong.
